newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen steadies, exhausted after Asian rebound.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen steadies, exhausted after Asian rebound.

text.p: The dollar steadied in Europe, exhausted after rebounding as much as four percent in Asia as Eisuke Sakakibara, a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official, allayed concern about trade tensions between U.S. and Japan.
Sakakibara, the director general of the Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said the issue of U.S.-Japan trade relations was "being played up excessively."

He also said Japan's current account surpluses will not be a major point of discussion at the Group of Seven leading industrial nations meeting in Denver next week and reiterated Japan's readiness to combat excessive currency moves.

Traders who had bet the dollar would fall below the six-month low of 110.62 yen it set Wednesday were caught short by his comments and scrambled to cover their positions. Such buying drove the dollar to 115.70 yen, erasing the bulk of the losses it had racked up against the yen in the past four trading days.

"There seems to be a bit of froth building up given the size of the move, but it is quite clear that the Japanese don't want the dollar to go down any further," said Henry Wilkes, the head of trading at Bank Julius Baer.
The dollar was quoted at 114.09/45 yen at 1040 GMT, from 111.20/25 late Wednesday in Europe.
Dollar/mark was at 1.7232/35 from 1.7158/68 Wednesday, while mark/yen clambered up to 66.20/23 from 64.82/85 yesterday.

Concern about the potential for trade tensions between the U.S. and Japan was sparked after U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said Wednesday Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth.

Sakakibara's verbal intervention has led traders to expect he will tone down any comments on trade he makes when he addresses the Computing Technology Industry Association conference at 1800 GMT today. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is also scheduled to speak today.

Rubin has already tried to assuage fears of U.S-Japan trade friction, saying Wednesday he agreed with Japan's goal of avoiding sustained increases in its external surpluses and promoting domestic demand-led growth. He also played down the importance of a short-term widening in Japan's surpluses.

"The U.S. and Japan are trying to firefight before it gets unmanageable," said Paul Meggyesi, the senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "You can expect to hear more backtracking on the trade front today."
Trade worries may return to the fore, with President Bill Clinton due to meet top auto executives on June 27.
Still, analysts expect expectations of higher U.S. interest rates to support the dollar, particularly since they already offer a substantial premium over German and Japanese rates.

"Trade may be working against the dollar, but interest rates should work in the dollar's favour," said Meggyesi at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "The market is jumping the gun by looking for a Japanese rate hike."

Federal Reserve Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin said Wednesday it was a "close call" as to whether the Fed would act at its July policy meeting to slow growth to more sustainable levels than the 5.8 percent annual rate seen in the first quarter of 1997.

Also, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said Thursday a half-percentage point increase in U.S. rates may be needed in mid-1997 to slow growth. The target fed funds rate is now at 5.5 percent.

Dollar/mark is already benefiting from expectations France will agree next week to the budget deficit stability pact which requires countries to observe fiscal discipline after they join European economic and monetary union.
European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said Thursday he believed a deal would be reached at the EU summit in Amsterdam next week.

"A stability pact looks set to be signed next week and the mark is looking a little weak," said David Bloom, currency strategist at HSBC James Capel. - Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
